lines.text: Drive to Point only works if the robot knows where it's standing. A camera is how it finds out, and none of this is code yet.
Wheels lose a little ground the longer you drive, and they never get it back. A tag sits at a known place on the field, so a sighting late in a match is as good as one at the start.
It isn't a replacement, though. Sightings come now and then, and they're noisy, so the robot keeps its odometry and blends the two.
We use a Limelight, with the camera and processor in one sealed unit. On PhotonVision, the ideas still carry over.
Pick the mounting spot by thinking about the moment you score. That's when the pose has to be right, so that's when the camera needs a tag in view.
Seen straight on from its own height, a tag is a plain rectangle, and a tiny error in one corner swings the answer a long way. From off to one side, the shape tells the camera far more.
On the Limelight 3 and 4, we've found the lens doesn't come glued, so you may want to glue yours.
Six steps, and the order matters. The field map comes first, because a camera still running last season's map puts every tag in the wrong spot.
Then the AprilTag pipeline, since a color pipeline never reports a position at all. Turn the exposure down as far as the camera can stand, so a moving robot doesn't blur the tag.
The camera only ever solves for where the camera is. The offsets move that answer to the middle of the robot, so if they're wrong, every reading is off the same way.
Calibration takes out the bend in the lens, which is worst near the edges of the picture. Then write down the camera's name, because that's how the code will find it.
Now test it. Hold a tag about a meter out and check the distance against a tape measure. Once they agree, the code can start feeding these sightings into the pose.
